candidates.title: Nebius Lifts 2026 CapEx View to $27B: Can Funding Keep Pace?
candidates.snippet: Nebius Lifts 2026 CapEx View to $27B: Can Funding Keep Pace? The Globe and Mail
candidates.text:
This section contains press releases and other materials from third parties (including paid content). The Globe and Mail has not reviewed this content. Please see disclaimer .
Nebius Lifts 2026 CapEx View to $27B: Can Funding Keep Pace?
Zacks Investment Research - Zacks Investment Research - Thu Nov 19, 11:23AM CST
Nebius Group N.V . NBIS is pursuing an aggressive capacity expansion strategy as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure remains robust. The company raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to approximately $27 billion from the earlier projected range of $20-$25 billion.
Nebius spent nearly $7.3 billion in capex in the third quarter of 2026 on server and network equipment and data center footprint expansion. However, the substantial spending requirements raise questions about the company's ability to finance its aggressive expansion plans.
Nebius is increasingly relying on customer prepayments to support infrastructure investments. The company expects $10 billion in committed customer prepayments in 2026. In the third quarter, more than 90% of the contract value signed carried prepayments. Notably, these payments covered more than 100% of the capex associated with newly contracted capacity, compared with 50-60% in the preceding quarter.
The company is also strengthening its funding position through asset-backed financing and capital market transactions. Nebius secured a $775 million asset-backed financing facility at SOFR plus 250 points in July 2026, supported by long-term customer agreements. Management sees more than $40 billion in similar committed revenues from investment-grade customers as supporting further asset-backed financing opportunities. In October, Nebius announced a $3.5 billion senior secured financing facility with Citi to support its global infrastructure expansion.
Nebius Group N.V. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Nebius Group N.V. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Nebius Group N.V. Quote
Also, in the third quarter, NBIS issued 4.6 million Class A shares at a weighted average price of $229.1 per share, generating net proceeds of approximately $1 billion under its at-the-market ("ATM") equity program. NBIS considers ATM as a flexible funding tool.
Looking ahead, Nebius expects capex to increase further to $40-$45 billion in 2027, supporting the addition of more than 1 gigawatt of new capacity. Management anticipates that customer prepayments of $17-$20 billion and asset-backed financing will cover 75-85% of planned 2027 capex.
Despite these financing arrangements, the magnitude of investments remains a concern.
Though customer prepayments and diversified financing sources provide meaningful support, the payoff hinges on execution, continued AI demand and the ability to scale profitably amid increasing competition from the likes of CoreWeave CRWV and tech giants like Microsoft MSFT and Amazon.
Competitors Ramp Up CapEx Amid AI Infrastructure Buildout
CoreWeave ’s third-quarter capex reached $14.5 billion, while 2026 capex is now expected to be between $37 billion and $39 billion (from $35-$39 billion previously), considerably exceeding projected annual revenues. The company expects full-year 2026 revenues to be $13-$13.3 billion. Such aggressive spending exposes CoreWeave to execution risks if infrastructure deployments face delays or demand moderates.
Third-quarter operating expenses came in at $3.5 billion from $1.31 billion in the year-ago quarter, reflecting the cost of scaling active power and converting backlog into revenues. On the earnings call, management said that it expects approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the following three months, providing funding support.
Microsoft ’s capex spend far exceeds the combined capex plans for both Nebius and CoreWeave for 2026. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, capital expenditures reached $45.2 billion, with roughly three-fourths directed toward short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, including higher memory and storage costs. Microsoft added 24 data centers across five continents during the quarter.
The company expects capex to exceed $50 billion in the fiscal second quarter. Capex is now projected to be approximately $170 billion for calendar 2026, given the third-party capacity delays. The company expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027.
NBIS Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates
Nebius stock has lost 37.7% in the past month compared with the Zacks Internet – Software and Services industry’s decline of 11%.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
NBIS’ shares are trading at a 12-month forward price/sales multiple of 2.42X, below the Internet Software Services industry’s 3.42X.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NBIS’ earnings for 2026 has been significantly revised upward over the past 60 days.
Image Source: Zacks Investment Research
NBIS currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.
Beyond Nvidia: AI's Second Wave Is Here
The AI revolution has already minted millionaires. But the stocks everyone knows about aren't likely to keep delivering the biggest profits. AI’s second wave is moving from infrastructure to implementation and these companies are at the forefront of this transition, positioned to become what Amazon and Google were to the internet era. candidates.title: Inox Clean, Blupine, Serentica corner 35% of $3.85 billion funding raised by Indian energy startups in 2026
candidates.snippet: Inox Clean, Blupine, Serentica corner 35% of $3.85 billion funding raised by Indian energy startups in 2026 ET EnergyWorld
candidates.text:

Inox Clean, Blupine, Serentica corner 35% of $3.85 billion funding raised by Indian energy startups in 2026
The three companies together raised $1.36 billion in 2026 YTD, accounting for the bulk of the disclosed funding raised during the period, as per Tracxn data analysed by ETEnergyWorld.
Ritik Raj
ETEnergyWorld
Published On Nov 19, 2026 at 01:17 PM IST

Image for representational purposes only Indian energy startups and companies raised around $3.85 billion in disclosed funding across 178 equity and debt transactions between January 1 and November 17, 2026, with Inox Clean Energy , Blupine Energy and Serentica Renewables accounting for nearly $1.36 billion of the total, according to Tracxn data analysed by ETEnergyWorld.
The three companies together accounted for around 35 per cent of the disclosed funding during the period. The data covers companies operating across the energy and energy technology sectors in India.
Tracxn lists 160 transactions with disclosed funding amounts, while 18 transactions have been marked undisclosed.
Advt
Inox Clean Energy, Blupine Energy and Serentica lead fundraising Blupine Energy topped the three companies with $594.42 million raised through a conventional debt transaction in January. Axis Bank was listed as the investor in the funding round.
On the other hand, Serentica Renewables raised $345 million through a conventional debt round in July. The funding involved the Asian Development Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, New Development Bank (NDB) and Exim Bank.
Inox Clean Energy raised a combined $417.46 million across two transactions in 2026. The company secured $343.82 million in a Series D round in January, with CalPERS, SUN Group Global and Authum among the institutional investors. Akash Bhansali was also listed among the angel investors. It raised another $73.64 million in July, with Rising Sun Holdings listed as an investor.
Resolven, Simple Energy, Rideriver among other major fundraisers Beyond the three largest contributors, Resolven and Simple Energy emerged as major fundraisers. Resolven raised $209.33 million across two transactions, including a $161.07 million Series A round led by Zest Bidco and $48.26 million through conventional debt from NIIF IFL.
Simple Energy raised $206.25 million across three transactions. Its largest funding round was a $180 million Series C investment in September, led by Dr A Velumani Family Office. Arokiaswamy Velumani led its earlier $13.33 million Series B round.
Rideriver raised $123.60 million across four transactions, including a $102 million Series C round jointly led by Elev8 Venture Partners and Claypond Capital. GreenCell Mobility raised $123.47 million across two transactions, including $89 million in debt funding from IFC, British International Investment and Tata Capital.
Advt
GREW Solar secured $115.88 million in a Series D round led by Bay Capital, while Hygenco raised $105 million in Series C funding led by IFC, with Siemens and Fullerton Carbon Action Fund also participating.
AMPIN Energy Transition and Radiance Renewables each raised $100 million. Norfund was listed as an investor in AMPIN's Series E round, while Impact Fund Denmark and FMO participated in Radiance Renewables' Series C funding.
Other notable fundraises during the period included Yulu's $93 million across two transactions, with GEF Capital Partners leading its $63 million Series C round, and Ultraviolette's $87.47 million across two transactions. Its $85 million Series E round in September was jointly led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.

candidates.title: Fintech Payhawk raises $280 mn in Series C funding at $2 bn valuation
candidates.snippet: Fintech Payhawk raises $280 mn in Series C funding at $2 bn valuation Beinsure
candidates.text:
Agentic AI News
InsurTech News
🇪🇺 Europe Insurance News
Payhawk expands AI agents across corporate finance
Goldman Sachs Alternatives backs international expansion
Finance Operating System integrates AI, payments and controls
Payhawk reports positive cash flow and subscription-led revenue
Fintech Payhawk has secured $280 mn in Series C funding led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, valuing the financial technology company at $2 bn.
The round brings total capital raised to more than $515 mn. Existing investors QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures participated alongside new investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, as well as European entrepreneurs Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee.
Founded in Sofia, Bulgaria, Payhawk now operates in 33 countries through 12 offices. Its platform supports multiple currencies, banking systems, payment networks and regulatory requirements, reflecting the complexity of managing corporate finance across international markets.
Payhawk secured $280 mn in Series C financing led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, reaching a $2 bn valuation and bringing total funding to more than $515 mn.
The fintech operates across 33 countries with 12 offices and plans to develop an AI-powered Finance Operating System combining autonomous agents, payment infrastructure and enterprise controls.
Payhawk achieved positive cash flow in Q3 and retains 70% of its 2022 funding. The company says 77% of customers use its AI agents daily.
The transaction remains subject to customary regulatory approvals. Payhawk plans to invest in a global Finance Operating System designed to automate financial operations using AI agents, integrated payments and enterprise controls.
Payhawk expands AI agents across corporate finance
Payhawk is developing AI agents that execute financial tasks across procurement, business travel, financial control and reporting. The company reports that 77% of its customers use these agents daily to reduce administrative work and operating costs.
The role of the finance team is rapidly moving away from manual checks, lengthy reconciliations and labor-intensive work towards becoming more strategic. While most companies use AI to speed up existing processes, we built AI agents to fundamentally rethink how finance operates.
Hristo Borisov, co-founder and CEO of Payhawk
Payhawk describes its objective as “zero-touch finance”, in which routine administrative tasks can be completed without direct intervention from finance professionals or employees.
Borisov said achieving this requires AI capabilities to operate alongside payment infrastructure and controls governing financial transactions.
Goldman Sachs Alternatives backs international expansion
James Hayward, Managing Director within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, will join Payhawk’s Board of Directors.
Hayward cited Payhawk’s engineering capabilities, international operations and approach to enterprise spend management as factors behind the investment.
Payhawk’s exceptional growth reflects the strength of its engineering DNA, global footprint and clear vision for the future of modern spend management systems.
Borisov said the company’s European origins helped it develop products for businesses operating across different jurisdictions. “Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else. We should build categories the rest of the world follows as craftsmanship and innovation are strongly embedded cultural traits for Europeans,” he said.
The company intends to use its existing international infrastructure to support multinational customers managing financial operations across several markets.
Finance Operating System integrates AI, payments and controls
Payhawk’s Finance Operating System is structured around three interconnected components: AI agents that perform financial tasks, payment infrastructure that enables transactions, and enterprise controls that determine authorization requirements and when human approval is necessary.
The platform is intended to connect automated financial processes with execution and oversight.
Enterprise resource planning systems, banks, procurement platforms, treasury applications and travel management software increasingly use Model Context Protocol (MCP) to make information accessible to AI applications.
Payhawk argues that connecting these systems does not necessarily automate the financial processes spanning them.
“Integrations connect systems. MCP makes information easier to access. But an operating system changes how the entire finance function works,” Borisov said. “As software moves from recommending actions to actually taking them, that distinction becomes much more important.”
Payhawk reports positive cash flow and subscription-led revenue
Payhawk achieved positive cash flow in Q3 and retains 70% of the capital raised in its previous funding round in 2022. Its business model relies on subscription revenue rather than interchange fees from corporate card transactions.
The company says this allows it to develop financial automation products independently of card spending volumes.
In the US, Payhawk’s Financial Controller Agent works with customers’ existing business cards, removing the need to change providers or reissue cards.
The Series C investment will support further development of Payhawk’s AI-based financial products and expansion of its international enterprise operations.
Peter Sonner
Lead Tech Editor
Peter Sonner is Lead Tech Editor at Beinsure, with more than 10 years of experience in digital media and financial technology reporting. He covers InsurTech and FinTech, startup funding, artificial intelligence, blockchain, cryptoassets, and digital transformation in insurance. Previously involved in the international team at SQL Stunts, USA Wire, Whisp Money, ISUR, Tresor Finance, and Forinsurer, he examines how emerging technologies and AI affect insurers.

candidates.title: Infranity Raises €1.5 Billion For Fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt Vintage
candidates.snippet:
Infranity has completed the final close of its fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt vintage, securing €1.5 billion across the strategy and associated co-investment vehicles.
The post Infranity Raises €1.5 Billion For Fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt Vintage appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Infranity Raises €1.5 Billion For Fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt Vintage
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 4:22 PM
Infranity Raises €1.5 Billion For Fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt Vintage
Infranity has completed the final close of its fourth Senior Infrastructure Debt vintage, securing €1.5 billion across the strategy and associated co-investment vehicles.
The fundraising met its target and attracted institutional investors, including repeat commitments from existing backers.
The manager has already made 16 investments through the vintage, financing European infrastructure assets and companies.
Its focus areas include energy transition, digital infrastructure, decarbonized mobility, environmental infrastructure, waste and water.
The strategy seeks long-term, risk-adjusted returns through senior debt, using credit selection and portfolio construction to manage exposure across those sectors.
The latest fund follows the previous vintage’s closing in 2023.
As of October 2026, Infranity’s Senior Investment Grade Infrastructure Debt strategy had raised more than €6.65 billion.
CEO and Managing Partner Philippe Benaroya said the latest close reflects both investor support and the platform’s pace of deployment.
The firm is preparing the next vintage and sees opportunities associated with higher lending margins and compensation for committing capital to less-liquid investments.
Those conditions represent management’s assessment of the market rather than a guarantee of returns.
Infranity is part of Generali Investments and specializes in infrastructure financing and investment.
Founded by Benaroya, Alban de La Selle and Gilles Lengaigne through a strategic partnership with Generali, the manager reported €15 billion in assets as of September 2026, measured as total investor commitments since inception.
Its broader investment activity includes infrastructure supporting energy, transport, digital connectivity, healthcare and education.
The fourth vintage adds another pool of capital to that platform, with deployment already underway and a further fundraising cycle being prepared.
The €1.5 billion headline includes co-investment commitments alongside the main vintage, rather than capital committed solely to one fund.
KEY QUOTE :
“The successful closing of the fourth vintage and its co-investment vehicles at its €1.5 billion target demonstrates the strength of Infranity’s European infrastructure debt platform. It reflects both our sustained deployment momentum and the continued confidence of our investors, including many existing investors who renewed their commitments. We are now preparing the next vintage of our flagship strategy, which we believe will enable investors to benefit from attractive market conditions, including higher margins and enhanced illiquidity premia.”
Philippe Benaroya, CEO And Managing Partner Of Infranity

candidates.title: Saudi Arabia’s Ceer raises $693 million as it builds a homegrown EV industry
candidates.snippet: Saudi Arabia’s Ceer raises $693 million as it builds a homegrown EV industry Fast Company Middle East
candidates.text:
Saudi Arabia’s homegrown electric vehicle maker Ceer has secured approximately $693 million (SR2.6 billion) to expand its operations, as the country works to build a domestic automotive industry.
The Public Investment Fund-owned company signed the financing agreement with Arab National Bank and Riyad Bank at its Riyadh headquarters. The funding will support its growth plans, according to a statement.
The Public Investment Fund-owned electric vehicle maker signed a financial agreement at its Riyadh headquarters. The financing will support its growth plans and the development of Saudi Arabia’s automotive manufacturing industry, according to a statement.
The country’s first homegrown automotive brand unveiled its first two flagship EVs in September, part of a planned portfolio of seven models over the next five years. The vehicles will be manufactured at Ceer’s production complex in Saudi Arabia.
“This agreement reflects ANB and Riyad Bank’s confidence in Ceer’s business model and long-term outlook,” said Joerg Schuessler, chief financial officer of Ceer. “Together, we are investing in the future of a Saudi automotive brand built for the Kingdom and its future economic ambitions.”
Ceer’s expansion forms part of a broader effort to build manufacturing capacity and bring more of the automotive supply chain into Saudi Arabia.
The National Industrial Development and Logistics Program targets an annual manufacturing capacity of 280,000 cars by 2030, along with the localization of 40% of the automotive value chain. That includes parts and components for both electric vehicles and internal combustion engine vehicles.
The ambition extends beyond assembling cars. Developing local suppliers would allow more of the spending associated with vehicle production to remain in the country.
By 2034, Ceer is projected to contribute $8 billion to Saudi Arabia’s gross domestic product and improve its trade balance by $21 billion, according to PIF.
Louai Al-Zaher, chief wholesale bank officer at Arab National Bank, said the agreement reflected the lender’s role in supporting promising sectors, particularly automotive manufacturing, and advancing Saudi Vision 2030.
Mohammed Abu Al-Naja, chief corporate banking officer at Riyad Bank, said the financing reaffirmed its commitment to “supporting national industries and advancing sustainable transport in line with Saudi Vision 2030 and the Saudi Green Initiative.”

candidates.title: Humanoid Robotics Sector Gains Momentum as Agile Robots Raises $500M and Agility Goes Public
candidates.snippet: Humanoid Robotics Sector Gains Momentum as Agile Robots Raises $500M and Agility Goes Public Metrology and Quality News
candidates.text:
Humanoid Robotics Sector Gains Momentum as Agile Robots Raises $500M and Agility Goes Public
November 19, 2026
Two significant developments in the humanoid robotics sector highlight growing investor confidence and accelerating commercial adoption, with Germany’s Agile Robots securing $500 million in new funding and US-based Agility Robotics completing its business combination to become a publicly listed company on Nasdaq.
The developments reflect increasing investment in Physical AI, as robotics companies move beyond research and demonstration projects towards commercial deployments in manufacturing, logistics and other industrial environments.
Agile Robots Raises $500 Million at $8.5 Billion Valuation
Munich-based Agile Robots has raised $500 million in a Series F funding round at a valuation of $8.5 billion. The investment was led by SoftBank Group, with participation from Nvidia, Hitachi Ventures and T. Capital.
The latest funding brings Agile Robots’ total capital raised to approximately $2 billion. The company intends to use the investment to increase production capacity, expand into key international markets and accelerate the development of new robotics applications.
Led by founder and CEO Dr. Zhaopeng Chen, Agile Robots develops and deploys Physical AI technologies, including humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and hands, alongside the software and AI models that enable them to perform increasingly complex industrial tasks.
Its technology is designed to automate operations that have traditionally depended on human dexterity and decision-making, with applications spanning automotive manufacturing, consumer electronics, healthcare and service industries.
Agile Robots reports more than 20,000 robotic solutions installed worldwide. The company plans to strengthen its presence in the United States while continuing to expand its manufacturing infrastructure in Germany.
In early 2026, it opened a new production facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich. The site has the capacity to manufacture up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually, providing additional capacity to meet anticipated demand.
Agility Robotics Becomes Publicly Listed Humanoid Robotics Company
Meanwhile, US-based Agility Robotics has completed its previously announced business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI, beginning trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market. The transaction and associated financing arrangements generated approximately $465 million in gross capital before expenses, making Agility the first publicly listed US pure-play humanoid robotics company with established commercial deployments.
The company enters the public markets with nearly three years of real-world deployment experience, more than 65,000 hours of robot operation, committed multi-year customer orders and US-based infrastructure designed to support commercial manufacturing and deployment at scale.
Agility has secured more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit 5 humanoid robot, subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications.
“AI is moving beyond the digital world and into the physical world, creating new possibilities for how people and machines work together,” said Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics. “ At Agility, that future is already taking shape. Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks.”
Agility’s flagship Digit platform is designed to operate in environments built for people, undertaking repetitive and physically demanding tasks while helping businesses address persistent labour shortages.
Existing deployments include operations with global companies such as GXO Logistics, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada.
Expanding Industrial Applications
Agility’s commercial deployment programme continues to develop. Its partnership with GXO has recently been expanded to include two additional US logistics facilities, with deployments planned for early 2027. This builds on an existing operation in Georgia, where Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes.
The company has also signed a commercial agreement with AGCO for a Digit pilot expected to begin in 2027. Three additional enterprise manufacturing customers are participating in paid programmes focused on specific industrial applications. These include a major global automaker, a leading automotive technology and components developer, and a global consumer products manufacturer.
Agility reports an active pipeline of more than 30 prospective customers across automotive, manufacturing, aerospace, logistics, consumer products and defence.
Unveiled in September 2026, Digit 5 incorporates developments based on several years of customer experience. These include proprietary cycloidal actuator technology designed to support repetitive lifting of up to 50 pounds (approximately 23 kg), interchangeable end effectors and expanded manipulation capabilities intended to extend the range of industrial workflows that can be automated.
Early customer access is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of the year.
Physical AI, Safety and Manufacturing Scale
Agility is also developing its underlying robotics and Physical AI platform through collaborations with NVIDIA, FORT Robotics and Nyobolt.
Digit 5 is planned to use NVIDIA IGX Thor onboard computing, alongside integration of NVIDIA Halos safety technology. Its collaboration with FORT Robotics focuses on safety systems for industrial environments.
Battery technology is another area of development. Through its partnership with Nyobolt, Agility is incorporating ultra-fast charging technology designed to recharge Digit 5 in approximately nine minutes and support more than 20 hours of productive operation within a 24-hour period.
To support commercial expansion, Agility has invested in a US manufacturing and development infrastructure that includes RoboFab

Indian semiconductor startup Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-powered smart sensors.
The round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Micromax, Valour Capital, Gaingels and angel investors.

Startups across Africa, the Middle East and Israel raised a combined $169.5 million this week, based on disclosed funding rounds tracked by Techloy, with investor capital flowing mostly into AI security. The Week's Largest Startup Funding Rounds

GlassPoint, which moved its leadership team to the UAE this year, builds solar plants that supply factories with heat under long-term contracts. N.I.S. led the $24 million round, with MITO Tech Ventures joining, to set up operations in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Oman and hire senior staff.

Imagen Raises $100M to Recruit Radiologists
The AI-powered New York radiology practice will use the funding for clinical staff, infrastructure and technology.
Updated on Nov. 19, 2026 in Healthcare
Live Poll
Would you trust an AI-assisted radiology reading of your medical scan?
▲ Yes ▼ No
Imagen, an AI-powered radiology practice based in New York, raised $100 million to recruit radiologists and train AI models. The company also gained rights to up to 150 million additional imaging studies.
Why it matters
Medical scans are flooding hospitals while the number of radiologists is too few to handle them, making staffing and AI-assisted interpretation a pressing concern. Imagen's expansion reflects an effort to close that gap across the United States.
Imagen interprets more than 2 million studies annually across 28 states and has gained rights to up to 150 million additional imaging studies, including X-rays, CT, MRI and ultrasound. Its valuation, revenue and lead investor were not disclosed with the $100 million raise.
The players
Imagen
An AI-powered radiology practice based in New York that interprets imaging studies across 28 states using FDA-cleared AI tools.
Aidoc
A radiology artificial intelligence company that secured $150 million in April to fund its radiology AI platform.
Serge Sicular
A public figure associated with the company's leadership and strategy.
The details
Imagen will direct the $100 million toward clinical resources, operational infrastructure and technology, and its practice uses FDA-cleared AI tools. The company, established in 2015, employs more than 230 radiologists and cardiologists. Aidoc separately secured $150 million in April for its own radiology AI platform.
Timeline
Imagen was established in 2015.
Imagen's staff count doubled in the previous year.
Aidoc secured $150 million for its radiology AI platform in April.
Imagen's $100 million raise was published on November 19, 2026.
The coming few quarters are expected to clarify Imagen's next steps.
Healthcare Landscape
Imagen's model of pairing FDA-cleared AI tools with a large radiologist workforce extends the use of cleared radiology software into a full clinical service. Its growth reflects broader pressure on U.S. imaging capacity as scan volumes outpace the supply of radiologists.
Patients and referring clinicians across the United States may see faster imaging interpretation as AI-assisted radiology services expand. Expanded staffing could ease backlogs, though how these changes affect costs and access has not been disclosed.
The takeaway
Growing scan volumes make AI-assisted radiology services worth watching for faster results. Patients can ask their providers which imaging services use AI tools and how reads are reviewed.

candidates.title: Ex-Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal's Humyn Labs raises $47 million to record human work for robots
candidates.snippet: Ex-Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal's Humyn Labs raises $47 million to record human work for robots Indian Startup News
candidates.text:
Funding Fusion
News
Ex-Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal's Humyn Labs raises $47 million to record human work for robots
Sumit Vishwakarma
19 Nov 2026
18:50
IST
Follow Us
New Update
Bengaluru-based physical AI startup Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in a Series A round made up of equity and venture debt.
Advertisment
The $26 million equity tranche was led by Accel , with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading and angel investor Anita Pramoda, former CFO of Epic.
The $21 million venture debt tranche was led by Lighthouse Canton, with Trifecta Capital participating, the startup said . Equity accounts for roughly 55% of the total.
It has not disclosed its valuation.
Where the capital will go
Humyn Labs said it will use the capital to build what it calls deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, where robots can be tested in real-world settings. It will also put money into its capture hardware and its data processing engine, and expand its research and market presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul.
“ Physical AI will only be as good as the real-world data it learns from. This funding will help us strengthen our research, build trust with labs and enterprises, and expand our global presence. With a $10 billion opportunity emerging in data infrastructure, we aim to build a $1 billion annual revenue business and establish ourselves as a global leader in the space, ” said Manish Agarwal, co-founder of Humyn Labs.
Pratik Agarwal, Partner at Accel, said data and deployment “ are where the real moat will be built ” in physical AI .
What Humyn Labs does
Robots being built to work in homes, factories and warehouses need large volumes of footage showing how humans actually handle objects and move through physical spaces. Text and video scraped from the internet do not provide that.
Humyn Labs fills the gap with its own capture devices. Its head-worn camera, called egoS1, records people doing tasks from a first-person view. The device has global-shutter stereo cameras recording at 1080p and 30 frames per second, a field of view of over 130 degrees, with the startup's processing engine producing depth, 3D head motion and 21-point hand tracking, according to the startup .
Its software then validates and labels the footage, tracking hand movements and interactions with objects. The output consists of training-ready datasets covering sight, sound, motion and touch, with verified provenance, which robotics teams can integrate into their training pipelines.
“ A robot does not learn a job from the internet. It learns it from the person who has done it for twenty years, on the floor where it will be done, ” said Ishank Gupta, co-founder of Humyn Labs.
The startup runs data collection across more than 20 countries in Latin America, East Asia, and South and Southeast Asia, with Brazil, India and South Korea as its main hubs. It has 51 full-time employees, most of them in Bengaluru, and works with local partners in the countries where it collects data.
The $50 million ARR claim
Humyn Labs said it crossed $50 million in annualised revenue within six months of starting operations.
Agarwal told TechCrunch the startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October, has another $20 million in signed contracts, and a further $20 million in deals that are yet to be finalised. Those three figures together add up to $50 million, but combining past revenue, signed contracts and prospective deals does not establish annualised revenue.
It has 12 paying customers, spanning frontier AI labs, humanoid robotics companies and world-model developers, and about 90% of its revenue comes from the US, according to Gupta. The startup has not named its customers.
In April, Humyn Labs had announced a $20 million commitment to fund data collection across India, Southeast Asia, Latin America and West Asia. At the time it said it was expanding voice data capabilities across 33 languages, dialects and accents, and planned to launch Robotics Labs for simulation environments and world models.
The founders and KGeN
Founded in February 2026 by Agarwal, the former CEO of gaming company Nazara Technologies, and Gupta, a former AB InBev executive, the startup converts footage of people performing everyday tasks into training data for robots.
The two earlier co-founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN, a blockchain-based platform that verifies real users for AI, gaming and decentralised finance companies. KGeN raised $13.5 million in October 2025 from Prosus Ventures, Jump Crypto and Accel, taking its total funding to $43.5 million. Two of those backers, Accel and Prosus Ventures, are also in Humyn Labs' round.
KGeN's network of contributors across emerging markets helps Humyn Labs collect data inside people's homes, the founders told TechCrunch.
Recording people at work and at home to train machines has raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly for footage captured inside homes. Recordings in homes and factories can pick up personal information, which puts the focus on how consent is taken and how the data is stored.
Humyn Labs is one of several startups selling real-world human data to robotics developers. Its competitors include Mecka AI, XDOF, MicroAGI, Human Archive and BuildAI.

Australian startups raise from Series C to seed across five sectors
Quantum software, stroke robotics, cattle feed, insolvency AI and office drink dispensers: here are five Australian companies that announced funding this week. Q-CTRL raised US$290 million in a Ser…
Yajush Gupta
Funding | Investment · 20 Nov 2026 · 2 min read
☆ Save
Above Australian startups raise from Series C to seed across five sectors . Dynamic Business
Quantum software, stroke robotics, cattle feed, insolvency AI and office drink dispensers: here are five Australian companies that announced funding this week.
Q-CTRL raised US$290 million in a Series C
Sydney-based quantum software company Q-CTRL has raised US$290 million (A$415 million) in a Series C led by Salesforce Ventures, with significant participation from Bullhound Capital and Affinity Partners.
New investors include AMD Ventures, EDGE Group, MPower Partners, Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation and SPARX Asset Management. Returning backers include DCVC, In-Q-Tel, Lockheed Martin Ventures, Main Sequence and Square Peg.
The company says the round was oversubscribed, expanded twice and is the largest quantum-sector fundraise for a software-focused business. Salesforce Ventures first backed Q-CTRL in 2023, when it joined a US$27.4 million Series B extension .
Founded in 2017 by Professor Michael J. Biercuk, Q-CTRL builds AI-powered infrastructure software for quantum technology. Its main product, Ironstone Opal, is a quantum navigation system designed to work when GPS is unavailable.
Remedy Robotics raised US$62 million in a Series B
Remedy Robotics has raised US$62 million in a Series B led by DCVC.
New investors include UC Investments, Skip Capital and Hostplus, one of Australia’s largest pension funds. Existing investors Build Collective by Tony Fadell, Blackbird, Divergent Capital and KdT Ventures also took part. The company previously raised US$35 million across its seed and Series A rounds.
Remedy develops AI-enabled robotic systems for stroke and other cardiovascular procedures. Its N1 System completed what the company says were the world’s first fully remote neurointerventional procedures in October 2025, and it partners with the Australian Stroke Alliance.
The funds will go towards a planned pivotal clinical trial with the University of California and advancing towards FDA approval. The company is headquartered in San Francisco, and its CEO and co-founder is Dr David Bell.
Provectus Algae raised US$4.3 million in a Series A extension
Noosaville-based Provectus Algae has closed a US$4.3 million extension to its Series A, bringing total Series A funding to more than US$14 million.
At One Ventures led the original Series A. The extension welcomed Queensland Investment Corporation as a new investor, including through the Queensland Government’s A$30 million Sowing the Seeds of Farming Innovation Fund. The government’s share was A$2.8 million , which brings total state investment in the company to A$3.8 million.
Provectus Algae is an Australian biotechnology company that uses AI-enabled discovery and biomanufacturing to develop biological products for agriculture, crop protection and human nutrition. Founder and CEO Nusqe Spanton leads the company.
Its Surf’N’Turf cattle feed was trialled on more than 2,700 cattle with lot-feeder Mort & Co and showed a 67% reduction in methane. It is now being commercialised through Proteus Ag, with Queensland manufacturing capacity being scaled to supply 250,000 cattle in 2027.
Morgan AI raised A$3.65 million in a seed round
Hobart-based Morgan AI has raised A$3.65 million in a seed round led by Blackbird. SideStage Ventures, Archangel, TEN13, The Eights, BlackSheep and a group of insolvency industry experts also took part.
Founders Josh Abulafia and Elle Curran previously ran food delivery startup ChefPrep, later CoLab, which raised a $3 million seed round in 2022 and entered voluntary administration in 2023. They named Morgan after the EY insolvency practitioner who worked with them during that process.
The company is building an AI-based operating system for restructuring and insolvency work. It automates investigations, reporting and case management, and turns scattered financial records into structured data. WLP Restructuring is one of its design partners.
The funds will go towards hiring, product development and expansion into overseas markets, starting with the UK.
Refilled raised A$5.6 million in a Series A
Sydney startup Refilled has raised A$5.6 million in a Series A led by OIF Ventures. Existing investor Melt Ventures took part, along with a personal investment from fund manager David Paradice.
Melt also led Refilled’s A$1.3 million seed round in 2023, which included Envato co-founders Cyan and Collis Ta’eed. The company has now raised A$7.5 million in total.
Refilled makes Australian-built smart drink dispensers, called Refillers, that serve flavoured still and sparkling water to offices and hotels as an alternative to bottled drinks. The company emerged from the University of Technology Sydney, and customers include Google, Meta and Atlassian.

candidates.title: What The Telecom Bust Taught Me About AI’s Debt Boom
candidates.snippet: The AI buildout’s growing reliance on debt echoes the telecom bubble, raising the risk that infrastructure spending will outpace the revenue needed to meet fixed repayment obligations. According to guest author David Spreng of Runway Growth Capital, even if AI fulfills its technological promise, borrowers’ survival will depend on realistic demand forecasts and debt tied to dependable cash flows, with missed timelines potentially forcing restructurings and bankruptcies.
candidates.text:
Artificial intelligence • Communications tech • Startups • Venture
What The Telecom Bust Taught Me About AI’s Debt Boom
Guest Author
November 20, 2026
Guest Author
0
Shares
Email
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
By David Spreng
The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean.
There is an old story in Stephen Hawking ’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle. Asked what the turtle stands on, she replies that it’s “turtles all the way down.” Her response is what philosophers call infinite regress — a chain of claims in which each one rests on another of the same kind and solid ground never arrives.
David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital.
I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape. Valuations support borrowing, and borrowing builds capacity. The capacity then becomes proof that the valuations were right, so each claim stands on the one beneath it.
Over the past year, more of the stack has started running on debt rather than equity, and in my experience, that crossing is the moment the telecom bubble becomes the relevant history given that debt may change how these stories end.
Until recently, the AI buildout was largely an equity-financed story, with venture investment reaching record levels.
Crunchbase data shows global venture funding totaled $679 billion through the first three quarters of 2026, the highest amount ever recorded for that period. AI companies attracted $102 billion in the third quarter alone, accounting for roughly 64% of global venture funding. A record 27 companies raised rounds of $1 billion or more during the quarter, collectively accounting for about a third of that total.
Equity financing carries significant risks, but unlike debt, it generally does not impose fixed repayment obligations. When investments underperform, equity investors typically absorb losses through declining valuations, while companies may retain greater flexibility to pursue their long-term strategies.
That debt is now arriving in size. Meta sold $30 billion of bonds last October in one of the largest corporate debt sales on record , then returned for $25 billion more in April , with investors reportedly demanding more compensation the second time. Amazon , Alphabet and Oracle have each borrowed tens of billions of their own , and Meta’s giant Louisiana data-center campus was financed with a record $27 billion bond raised by a joint-venture partner rather than by Meta itself. Morgan Stanley expects the big AI and cloud companies to spend about $3 trillion on infrastructure through 2028, with only about half of it expected to come from their own cash flow. The rest has to come from somewhere, and increasingly I think that somewhere is the bond market and private credit.
I watched the earlier version of this from a front-row seat, first as a venture capitalist in the late 1990s and since then as a lender to growth-stage technology companies. Telecom borrowed staggering sums against a demand forecast that was widely repeated and rarely checked, the famous claim that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days .
Traffic was actually doubling about once a year, spectacular growth but a fraction of what the borrowing assumed. By 2002 the telecom sector carried roughly $1 trillion in debt , much of which the chairman of the FCC told Congress would never be repaid, and WorldCom had entered what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history .
Much of the fiber the industry laid sat dark for years and was finally put to work by buyers who paid pennies on the dollar for it in bankruptcy, through a decade of restructurings and private mergers that rebuilt entire cap tables. Some companies survived that process, and many did not.
The demand narrative
The echo that concerns me most is the demand narrative. Today’s version holds that data centers are effectively leased before they are built and that the only real mistake is building too little. That may prove correct, but it is repeated with the same uniformity the traffic forecast enjoyed in 1999, and much of it rests on projections supplied by the companies doing the building. What has changed in recent months is that investors have begun demanding an answer.
Anthropic is now public, and once companies of that scale report financial results every quarter, investors can check the demand story against audited numbers.
Some may argue, reasonably, that my comparison fails and that the companies doing the largest borrowing may be among the most profitable enterprises ever built, with cash flows the telecom carriers never approached. A few AI companies also appear to be reaching revenue scale faster than any businesses before them.
And the internet really did change everything, just as the traffic really did arrive. All of that may be true, and none of it answers the question I think a lender has to ask, which is whether the cash arrives on the schedule the debt requires. Equity can generally wait out a wrong timeline in a way debt cannot, and when borrowed money builds capacity faster than revenue arrives to service it, in my opinion, the correction tends to come through restructurings rather than quiet markdowns.
Enduring lessons
None of this is a prediction that the AI buildout must end the way telecom did. The most durable lesson of the telecom bust, in my view, concerned capital structure, which decided who was still standing when demand finally caught up with capacity, long after the technology itself had been vindicated. I have spent years arguing that growth companies fear debt more than they should , and I still believe it, but the argument has always been conditional.
Debt serves borrowers whose obligations are sized to revenue they can see and
